title: Graduation: Your XIOM Journey
story: You started knowing nothing about programming. You couldn't write a single line of code. Now look at you. 400+ lessons. Eight levels. You've built calculators, number guessing games, text adventures, unit converters, prime generators, quiz engines, bank simulators, RPG character builders, weather dashboards, Morse code translators, tic-tac-toe engines, expense trackers, word games, chess boards, and a full snake game. You know variables, functions, structs, enums, pattern matching, error handling, contracts, ownership, collections, generics, interfaces, and modules. You didn't just learn to code — you became a programmer. This final lesson isn't about new concepts. It's about you. Run this program. Watch the journey unfold. You earned this.
why: The graduation lesson is a celebratory capstone that reflects on the entire learning journey, uses every XIOM feature as a showcase, and prints a personalized 'diploma' summarizing achievements — closing the curriculum with pride and motivation to continue building.
analogy: Graduation day. You're wearing a cap and gown, holding a diploma that lists every course you completed, every skill you mastered, and every project you built. But this isn't a ceremony — it's a launchpad. The diploma isn't the end of learning; it's proof you can learn anything. Behind you: 420 lessons, 8 levels, games, tools, and applications. Ahead of you: everything you haven't built yet. You have the tools. You have the knowledge. You have the proof. Now go.
try_it: This isn't the end. It's the beginning. Go build something amazing. Add your own favorite programs to the list. Add a personalized message or a 'next project' idea. Modify the diploma style. Share this program with someone you know — teaching is the highest form of mastery. And remember: every professional programmer started exactly where you are right now. The only difference between you and them is time. Keep building.
tips: This lesson uses every XIOM feature: structs, enums, Vec, Map, functions, loops, match, contracts — all together
The diploma is self-referential — the program describes the journey that taught you to write the program
There is no 'next' — this is the final lesson. The curriculum is complete. What you build next is entirely up to you
common_mistakes: Thinking the journey is over — 420 lessons taught you the language, but building real projects teaches you software engineering
Underestimating what you've accomplished — most people never write a single line of code. You wrote a snake game from scratch
Stopping here — the best way to solidify knowledge is to build something YOU care about, not just assigned lessons
